performers: Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau, baritone; Berlin Philharmonic; Rudolf Kempe, conductor
intro: The sun rises after a child’s death, as though nothing has happened. Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau sings the opening Kindertotenlied with Rudolf Kempe and the Berlin Philharmonic; an oboe and horn begin it alone.

sections.label: A · Oboe, horn and sunrise
sections.mNote: Two wind lines precede the baritone

sections.label: A′ · The sun shines for everyone
sections.mNote: Flute and bassoon join the returning phrases

sections.label: B · Night and eternal light
sections.mNote: Horns take the vocal tune; violins climb

sections.label: A″ · A lamp goes out
sections.mNote: Oboe and flute recall the opening

cues.title: Oboe above a horn
cues.text: The oboe edges upwards by small steps; a horn answers below it. Mahler marks the music slow and melancholy. The strings wait. Fischer-Dieskau’s first line places the rising sun inside this spare wind duet.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, p. 3: Langsam und schwermütig; nicht schleppend. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rückert’s two children
cues.text: Friedrich Rückert’s children Luise and Ernst die on 31 December 1833 and 16 January 1834. In grief he writes more than four hundred poems, none meant for print. Mahler later picks five of them.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, Universal Edition introduction to Kindertotenlieder (autumn 2008), gives the two dates and the 400-odd poems, published after Rückert’s death: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027. The Mahler Foundation counts 428 poems and says they were not intended for publication: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/

cues.title: “Nur mir allein”
cues.text: “Das Unglück geschah nur mir allein” — the disaster happened to me alone. Rückert puts the whole distance between the father and the bright morning into those last three words. The opening tune returns, with the flute above the voice and the bassoon repeating its small upward steps.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 6–8, second couplet of Rückert’s poem; our translation. Geert Woltjer discusses the flute doubling and bassoon figure: https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Night inside the father
cues.text: The third couplet speaks to the father himself: he must sink his night into eternal light. Horns take up the earlier vocal melody, and the voice answers with a new line. The violins carry the climb onwards after the words run out.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 9–14. The third couplet and the exchange of oboe, horn and vocal phrases are discussed at https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One cycle, not five numbers
cues.text: A footnote on the first page of the score asks that the five songs be treated as one inseparable whole. Their continuity is to be kept, Mahler adds, even against the applause that would normally follow a “number”.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460 (1905), printed p. 3, footnote: “Diese 5 Gesänge sind als ein einheitliches, untrennbares Ganzes gedacht …”; our translation. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 The same instruction is printed on the title page of the 1905 vocal score: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtLprints.htm

cues.title: The extinguished lamp
cues.text: “Ein Lämplein verlosch in meinem Zelt” — a little lamp went out in my tent. Fischer-Dieskau returns to the opening melody with this small domestic image. Oboe and flute bring back their short phrases, and the glockenspiel sounds through the gaps.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 14–17, Rückert’s final couplet; our translation. Page 14 marks the orchestral return zurückkehrend.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A sold-out Musikverein
cues.text: On 29 January 1905 Mahler conducts the first performance of the cycle in the Kleiner Musikvereinssaal in Vienna, with Friedrich Weidemann as soloist. The concert sells out days beforehand, and tickets for the afternoon dress rehearsal go on sale. A repeat follows on 3 February.
cues.evidence: Paul Banks, The Music of Gustav Mahler: A Catalogue of Manuscript and Printed Sources, Kindertotenlieder: chronology (29 January and 3 February 1905, Kleine Saal des Musikvereins, concert of the Vereinigung schaffender Tonkünstler Wiens) and the first-performance note (sold out by 24 January, dress-rehearsal tickets released, repeat arranged): https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtL.htm

cues.title: Harp and small bells
cues.text: The baritone’s final word is “Welt” — world. The harp keeps its little rocking figure going, with soft glockenspiel notes above it. Mahler leaves the last bar empty under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 17: final vocal phrase, harp, glockenspiel and the closing bar of rests with fermatas. The existing cue marks the closing passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The oboe starts again
transitions.to: A′ · The sun shines for everyone
transitions.how: The harp’s rocking D-minor figure and glockenspiel notes continue beneath the oboe’s return. The second couplet shortens the introduction: flute joins the vocal line, while the bassoon takes the repeated C♯–D steps below. The singer’s rhythm changes to put the stress on “mir” — me.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 6–8; Woltjer, song I, discussion of bars 22 onwards. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html

transitions.title: The horn takes the tune
transitions.from: A′ · The sun shines for everyone
transitions.how: After “allgemein”, the horn stretches the closing phrase over low clarinet and bassoon notes. The oboe answers more urgently. In the passage that follows, the horn takes the first vocal tune while the singer moves against it; D minor and D major alternate as the words turn towards eternal light.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 9–13; Woltjer, song I, discussion of bars 36–59. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html

transitions.title: Flute and oboe find home
transitions.how: Marked zurückkehrend — returning — the flute’s running notes soften around the oboe’s opening phrase. Horns hold below; glockenspiel notes punctuate the retreat. The strings fall silent before the last couplet restores the D-minor vocal melody.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 14–15, zurückkehrend and the final couplet. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song I, printed pp. 3–17: oboe and horn introduction, muted strings, the violins’ rising phrases and the final harp and glockenspiel.

timeline.note: Opening duet: oboe above the first horn; the voice and strings wait.
Harp and muted violas and cellos accompany the baritone’s first stanza.
The oboe’s opening phrase returns as the father names the loss that belongs to him alone.
The first violins enter with a high melody as the voice turns towards eternal light.
Flute and oboe bring back the opening phrases before the last stanza.
Harp and strings accompany the father’s blessing of the world’s joyful light.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
